title: A Genius Without Memory. Why Don’t Octopuses Rule the Earth?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Bauckham, Richard, Jesus and the Eyewitnesses: The Gospels as Eyewitness Testimony, Eerdmans 2006, ch. 13
Brown, Peter C.; Roediger, Henry L.; McDaniel, Mark A., Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning, Harvard University Press 2014

Dean, Lewis G.; Kendal, Rachel L.; Schapiro, Steven J.; Thierry, Bernard; Laland, Kevin N., Identification of the Social and Cognitive Processes Underlying Human Cumulative Culture, “Science” 335 (2012)
Robison, Bruce; Seibel, Brad; Drazen, Jeffrey, Deep-Sea Octopus (Graneledone boreopacifica) Conducts the Longest-Known Egg-Brooding Period of Any Animal, “PLOS ONE” 9 (2014)
Roediger, Henry L.; Karpicke, Jeffrey D., Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention, “Psychological Science” 17 (2006)

paragraphs: Octopuses have about half a billion neurons, most of them located in their arms. Octopuses kept in aquariums can escape from a closed jar and recognize individual human keepers. And yet, for all their cleverness, they are incapable of managing other animals or building an underwater city. After laying her eggs, a female octopus cares for them devotedly and guards them, eating nothing the whole time, until finally she dies as soon as her young hatch. The young never meet their mother, and everything she learned in her lifetime is lost forever when she dies.

Compared with other animals, human beings lag behind in purely physical terms: a chimpanzee is stronger, and a dog is faster. What sets us apart, however, is the ability to write down our thoughts and pass on the skills we have gained to the generations that follow.

The Book of Joshua tells how the Israelites crossed the swollen Jordan on a dry riverbed. For many of them, the crossing of the Red Sea was only a family legend, but now they were facing a miracle of their own. Then comes a command that hardly anyone would have expected at such a dramatic moment. Twelve men, one from each tribe, are to go back to the very middle of the riverbed and each lift onto his shoulder a stone from the spot where the priests are still standing. When they reach the camp at Gilgal, Joshua sets up these stones as a lasting memorial and immediately explains the meaning of the whole undertaking: “In the future, when your children ask their fathers, ‘What is the meaning of these stones?’ you are to tell them, ‘Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground.’” (Joshua 4:21–22).

A pile of river stones explains nothing by itself, and that is exactly the point of this biblical idea. A child notices something unusual and starts asking, and an adult answers with a story. A memorial like this comes alive only when two generations meet beside it. And the Bible repeats this pattern many times.

Yet after the death of Joshua and the elders, the Book of Judges records that a generation arose who did not know the LORD or His works (Judges 2:10). Knowledge of God did not pass to the children by itself, even though the stones still lay at Gilgal.

Stories of God’s guidance travel through the world in the same way as the skills we learn: someone who has experienced something tells it to someone who asks. You, too, stand in the middle of this chain of generations. You come to know God partly through the testimony of others, and you can do things you did not invent yourself. One day someone younger will ask you about your story, too…
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: Which stories will be lost forever if I don’t pass them on?
challenge: Before you put down your phone or step away from your computer, think of one skill someone taught you, and in a short prayer thank God for that person.

paragraphs: In May 2007, a remotely operated research vehicle from the MBARI institute descended to the floor of the Monterey submarine canyon off the coast of California. At a depth of almost 1,400 meters, in water of about three degrees Celsius, the robot’s camera recorded a female deep-sea octopus clinging to a rocky ledge and covering a cluster of eggs with her body. The researchers returned to the spot eighteen times over four and a half years, and each time they found her in exactly the same place. When they tried to feed her, offering her a piece of crab, she turned away from it. With every visit the octopus grew smaller, her skin paled and sagged, and her eyes clouded over. She was last seen in September 2011. A month later, only empty egg casings remained on the rock. The brooding had lasted 53 months, longer than in any other known animal.

The young of this species hatch large and ready to live on their own, yet they never meet their mother: her death coincides with their birth. Nothing she learned in her whole life is passed on to them.

This is the fate of most octopuses. And yet they are among the cleverest and most intelligent animals in the sea. So why is it not they who build underwater cities and make their own history, when their minds seem to be crying out for more?

sections.heading: Cleverness That Dies with Its Owner
paragraphs: The common octopus has about half a billion neurons, nearly two-thirds of them in its arms. Octopuses living in aquariums can escape from a closed jar and recognize individual human keepers. But they live short lives, usually a year or two. A female lays eggs once in her life and dies soon after her young hatch. Each octopus starts from zero, and whatever it discovers disappears with it. There is no mother to show it anything, and no grandfather to tell it a story.

Compared with other animals, human beings lag behind in purely physical terms: a chimpanzee is stronger, and a dog is faster. But we have something that no other creature has on such a scale. We can store knowledge outside our own minds and pass it on. Each generation starts where the previous one left off, and then adds its own brick. Researchers call this cumulative culture. You would simply say that someone taught you something.

Where does this human advantage come from? In 2012, scientists at the University of St Andrews in Scotland set out to find out. In their experiment, they gave an identical task to animals, chimpanzees and capuchin monkeys, and to humans: three- and four-year-olds from Scottish preschools. Each group was given the same box, which had to be opened in three stages, and every level completed brought a more attractive reward. The results were striking. The chimpanzees puzzled over it for thirty hours, but out of thirty-three of them only one made it all the way to the end. The capuchins gave up entirely: after fifty-three hours, not one had opened the box. The children needed only two and a half hours, and almost half of them completed the whole task. Individually, the children did not seem any cleverer. The difference lay in what they did together. They showed one another what worked, told one another what to press, and shared their rewards. The apes and monkeys each worked for themselves.

sections.heading: Memories Live Only in Stories
paragraphs: The knowledge that passes between people begins in a single mind, and that mind works quite differently from the way most students hope it does the night before an exam.

In 2006, psychologists Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke of Washington University in St. Louis ran an experiment: they gave students a short popular-science text to read. The first group was to read it four times. The second read it only once, but then three times wrote down from memory everything they could recall. The result? On a test given right after the study session, those who had only read did better. A week later, however, the picture was dramatically reversed. The readers now remembered only 40 percent of the material, while the students who had been made to work at recalling it remembered as much as 61 percent. Interestingly, it was the people who had gone over the text again and again who felt most confident of success. Repeated reading gives us the false impression that we already know it all. After a week, though, far more had stayed in the heads of the students who had to actively pull information out of their memory.

Telling the story of past events works in exactly the same way, because it, too, means actively pulling information out of memory. A perfect illustration of this mechanism is a story that the well-known biblical scholar Richard Bauckham cites in one of his books. In June 1901, a local newspaper in the English county of Norfolk reported the tragic death of a fisherman from the seaside village of Winterton. More than seventy years later, in 1973, an 83-year-old resident of the same village recalled the event in a recorded interview. In the year of the tragedy he had been just ten years old. Although after all those decades he got the year wrong, he gave the months and the whole course of events without a mistake, matching the newspaper report from long before. Bauckham points to two reasons for this: the event itself was deeply moving, and the memory had probably been told over and over again, both by the witness himself and in his presence. It was these two factors that allowed the story to survive in human memory for more than seven decades.

sections.heading: Twelve Stones from the Riverbed
paragraphs: The Bible knows this mechanism well and uses it on the scale of whole generations. In the story told in the Book of Joshua, the people of Israel stand on the bank of the Jordan, right across from Jericho. It is harvest time, so the river is in flood and has overflowed its banks. As soon as the priests carrying the Ark dip their feet in the water, the current flowing from upstream suddenly stops. The people cross to the other side on completely dry ground. The priests stand firm in the middle of the riverbed until the last person has safely left the river (Joshua 3:14–17).

Then comes a command that hardly anyone would have expected at such a dramatic moment. Twelve men, one from each tribe, are to go back to the very middle of the riverbed and each lift onto his shoulder a stone from the spot where the priests are still standing (Joshua 4:1–8). When they reach the camp at Gilgal, Joshua sets up these stones as a lasting memorial and immediately explains the meaning of the whole undertaking. “In the future, when your children ask their fathers, ‘What is the meaning of these stones?’ you are to tell them, ‘Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground.’” (Joshua 4:21–22).

A pile of river stones explains nothing by itself, and that is exactly the point of this biblical idea. A child notices something unusual and starts asking, and an adult answers with a story. A memorial like this comes alive only when two generations meet beside it. And the Bible repeats this pattern many times. Both in the account of the Passover in Exodus (Exodus 12:26–27; 13:14) and in the giving of the commandments in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 6:20–21), the same formula keeps coming back: a son who will one day come and ask.

But there is a detail in this story worth looking at, one that often escapes our notice. Many of the people standing by the Jordan that day had been born during the wandering in the wilderness. Their fathers, who remembered Egypt, had died along the way, and only the next generation reached the goal (Joshua 5:4–7). For them, the parting of the Red Sea was only a family legend or a flash of early childhood memory. Only now, when they themselves have crossed the river on dry ground, does Joshua bind these two worlds together. He reminds them that the LORD their God dried up the Jordan “just as He did to the Red Sea” (Joshua 4:23). In this way, the old story and their fresh, personal experience become one powerful foundation, which they will pass on to the generations to come.

The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month (Joshua 4:19). Exactly forty years earlier, on the same day of the year, families in Egypt had chosen a lamb for the first Passover (Exodus 12:3). Four days later, at Gilgal, the feast was celebrated for the first time in the new land (Joshua 5:10). The children who had just been asking what the river stones meant could, only a few days later, hear the second part of the same story at the festive meal.

Did this mechanism work? The Book of Judges answers that question without any embellishment. The people stayed faithful to God as long as the elders were alive who had seen His works with their own eyes (Judges 2:7). Then “another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10). The biblical text does not explain exactly what went wrong in this relay between generations. It only shows that knowledge of God and the memory of the past do not pass to children by themselves.

sections.heading: A Chain You Are Part Of
paragraphs: Faith is not passed down in our genes. Every generation could start from scratch, like the young octopuses on the canyon floor. The God of the Bible clearly reckons with this, which is why, alongside the commandments, He gives Israel tangible signs, stones and feasts, meant to prompt questions. God wants to be known for what He has done for real people in a particular place. And that kind of knowledge can only be passed on by someone who has experienced it, to someone who is looking for answers.

As someone who has received this knowledge and will one day pass it on, you stand right in the middle of this chain of generations. You carry within you the work of others, from the alphabet to the way your grandmother sliced bread. You can do things you did not invent yourself, because someone took the trouble to show you. Remember that one day someone younger will ask the same of you.

The same principle applies to your own story with God. We have a natural tendency to dwell on the hard moments, while the good ones easily fade into the grayness of everyday life. The Israelites carried the stones from the Jordan on their own shoulders. In the same way, the memory of God’s help can be a weight that has to be lifted deliberately and with effort. Some people write such moments down in a notebook. Others tell them at the table until the whole family knows them by heart. No one has to do this for God’s sake, since He remembers everything without our help. We do it for ourselves and for those who will come after us.

The nearest living source of memory is within arm’s reach. The older members of our families, or the neighbors across the landing, carry skills and stories that no one has ever written down. When they are gone, more than just memories disappears with them. For memory lives in people who share their stories. Even stories written down in a book or saved on a phone lie like the stones at Gilgal, waiting patiently for someone at last to ask about them and for someone else to tell them.

The same principle applies to learning new things. If you really want to remember something, actively pull it out of your memory. And if you want to pass some knowledge on, make room for the question someone younger will ask. You don’t need the brilliant memory of a master for this. It is enough to keep coming back to the things that matter most to you, and simply to talk about them out loud.

questions: Which stories will be lost forever if I don’t pass them on?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Think of one skill that someone taught you. It might be riding a bike or your first prayer. Picture the face of that particular person and thank God for them in one simple sentence.

**In action.** This week, visit an older person from your family or your neighborhood and ask them for one of two things. Ask them to show you how to make something with their own hands, such as cooking their signature dish or fixing something. Or ask them to tell you about one day in their life that changed something. Listen, and ask about the details. In the evening, write it down in a few sentences or record it, and then tell it to someone else. If you have no one to visit, call someone. And if even that is impossible today, simply write down one story someone once told you, before you lose it forever.
